newsitem.title: UK: Now Britain's serious parties provide the fun.
newsitem.headline: Now Britain's serious parties provide the fun.

text.p: The entertainment in British elections has traditionally been provided by the fringe "loony" candidates, but this time it is the mainstream parties that are supplying all the fun.

With the ruling Conservatives and the main opposition Labour Party virtually indistinguishable on a whole range of issues, the campaign for the May 1 election has become something of a policy-free zone.

What has filled the vacuum has been a series of ever more improbable stories loosely grouped under the heading of "sleaze", a catch-all term for sex and money scandals, usually involving members of the Conservative Party.
Britain's longest-serving party leader is Screaming Lord Sutch of the Monster Raving Loony Party, who campaigns under the slogan "Vote for insanity, you know it makes sense".

But does it make sense for Labour and the minority Liberal Democrats to stand down their candidates in the constituency of a former government minister accused of corruption in favour of a veteran BBC war correspondent who knows little of politics?

With polls suggesting the election could end the 18-year Conservative revolution started by Margaret Thatcher, the biggest news story of the campaign so far has been the surprise emergence of Martin Bell as an "anti-sleaze" candidate.

Bell, best known to television viewers for his reports from the Bosnian front lines, took to the campaign trail dressed in his trademark lucky white suit and green socks and immediately ran into worse flak than he ever found in a war zone.

Neil Hamilton, the former minister who denies taking money in return for asking questions in parliament, flanked by his formidable wife Christine, ambushed Bell's first news conference in the Tatton constituency in northwestern England.
They demanded, and got, from Bell an admission that Hamilton deserved to be considered innocent of corruption charges until proven guilty.
It was a confrontation that must have left Bell, who has covered wars from Vietnam to Bosnia, wondering what he has got himself into.
"I've still got my white suit on," he said later. "This is the scariest thing that has ever happened to me."

If it was scary for him, the whole episode has proved a headache for the Conservative leadership, struggling to get "sleaze" off the election agenda after a series of highly embarrassing stories in the newspapers.

Officials could cope with photographs of a Conservative MP in the company of a 17-year-old nightclub hostess and news that a prominent party member in Scotland had cited "a personal indiscretion" as a reason for not taking up a vacant seat.
But voters were then treated to the even odder spectacle of a Conservative member of parliament calling for the resignation of the Health Secretary, a party colleague.

"I'm not saying there should be a change of government. I do think there should be a change of minister," said MP Sir John Gorst, who alleged Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell had not played fair over the closure of an emergency ward in a hospital in Gorst's constituency.
Along with human antics, humans dressed as chickens have been major stars in this loony-tunes campaign where virtual reality wins every time over real politics.

The usually sober Conservatives sent a man-sized fowl on the road to pursue Labour leader Tony Blair, taunting him as "chicken" for not debating Prime Minister John Major. A headless version also joined Major on the trail, signifying his party's alleged lack of leadership.

With the election campaign now at its halfway mark, the major parties believe they are finally getting down to serious matters -- the current hot issue is which party can be trusted to run the country.
Some voters, confronted by the shenanigans in Tatton and elsewhere, are not so sure.
"Surely what's needed is a man in a white coat, not a man in a white suit," one disillusioned voter said.
